Parsing record wise

73| *

74| * To parse a CSV input from a file, you write: 75| *

76| * 77| * 
   78|  * File csvData = new File("/path/to/csv");
   79|  * CSVParser parser = CSVParser.parse(csvData, CSVFormat.RFC4180);
   80|  * for (CSVRecord csvRecord : parser) {
   81|  *     ...
   82|  * }
   83|  *
84| * 85| *

86| * This will read the parse the contents of the file using the 87| * RFC 4180 format. 88| *

89| * 90| *

91| * To parse CSV input in a format like Excel, you write: 92| *

93| * 94| * 
   95|  * CSVParser parser = CSVParser.parse(csvData, CSVFormat.EXCEL);
   96|  * for (CSVRecord csvRecord : parser) {
   97|  *     ...
   98|  * }
   99|  *
100| * 101| *

102| * If the predefined formats don't match the format at hands, custom formats can be defined. More information about 103| * customising CSVFormats is available in {@link CSVFormat CSVFormat Javadoc}. 104| *

105| * 106| *

Parsing into memory

107| *

108| * If parsing record wise is not desired, the contents of the input can be read completely into memory. 109| *

110| * 111| * 
  112|  * Reader in = new StringReader("a;b\nc;d");
  113|  * CSVParser parser = new CSVParser(in, CSVFormat.EXCEL);
  114|  * List<CSVRecord> list = parser.getRecords();
  115|  *
116| * 117| *

118| * There are two constraints that have to be kept in mind: 119| *

120| * 121| *
    122| *
  1. Parsing into memory starts at the current position of the parser. If you have already parsed records from 123| * the input, those records will not end up in the in memory representation of your CSV data.

  2. Parsing into memory may consume a lot of system resources depending on the input. For example if you're 125| * parsing a 150MB file of CSV data the contents will be read completely into memory.
